WORRY GUIDE — LOVE

When you're torn about breaking up

Your feelings for them remain, yet you don't know whether it's all right to go on like this. With breaking up, the more you think with your head, the further the answer can recede. The time you've spent together, the memories, and the life ahead of you are all involved — which is exactly why it's natural to feel torn. On this page, we'll look at angles for thinking about whether to continue or end a relationship, and tarot cards that reflect those feelings.

POINT 01

What's making this hard

In being torn over breaking up, "feelings for the other person" and "unease about the relationship" often exist separately. You haven't come to dislike them, yet being together is painful. Or perhaps you're only continuing because you're afraid to leave. When feelings like these mix, you can lose sight of what you yourself want. The loneliness of being alone, explaining it to those around you, and not wanting the years so far to go to waste also weigh on the judgment. Start by writing out, separately, "the other person," "how the relationship is," and "your own anxiety."

POINT 02

How to sort it out

When sorting it out, the viewpoint of "not assuming the other person will change" is useful. Conditional hope — I could continue if they changed in this way — wears you down each time the expectation misses. Try thinking about whether, with the other person exactly as they are now, you could spend your days calmly. It's also an important point to check whether anything remains that you haven't communicated in conversation. Whether things don't change even after you've told them, or whether you haven't told them yet, changes what you should do. And don't forget to turn your eyes to feelings that have continued over months, rather than a temporary wave of emotion.

POINT 03

How to read the cards

When you're torn over breaking up, cards that stand for "holding back," "loss," "letting go," and "bond" can offer clues.

The Two of Swords shows a figure blindfolded, holding both swords, postponing the decision.

The Two of Cups points to a relationship in which hearts connect equally,

and the Five of Cups points to a state in which, taken up by what was lost, you can't see what remains.

The Devil reflects an attachment in which you can't leave, even though you don't want it. Seeing which card is closest to you now, you'll start to see the outline of your honest feelings — whether you want to continue, or whether you want to leave but can't.

POINT 04

Questions to ask yourself

Try answering the following questions honestly. Within this relationship, how much of the time can you be yourself? Is there an honest feeling you haven't told the other person — and if you told them, what do you think would happen? Is your reason for not choosing to break up love for the other person, or anxiety about being alone? If you were carrying the same indecision a year from now, could you accept that? If a trusted friend were in the same situation, what words would you offer them? You don't have to produce an answer right away. Facing the questions itself becomes preparation for the decision.

CARDS

Cards connected to this decision

  • Two of Swords

    A card that reflects a state of closing your eyes and postponing the decision.

  • Two of Cups

    A clue for thinking about what a relationship in which hearts connect equally is.

  • Five of Cups

    A viewpoint for turning your eyes not only to what was lost, but to what remains.

  • The Devil

    It stands for attachment and dependence — being unable to leave even though you don't want it.

  • Three of Swords

    It shows that acknowledging the pain in your heart is the first step toward recovery.

  • Death

    A card that holds the meaning of a dividing line: an ending is also the next beginning.

Continue the relationship, or break up? Why not sort out the feelings you want to treasure, using the questions the cards raise?
